name: Ethan Brooks
body: We pointed existing S3 clients at RustFS and kept the same bucket layout. Throughput has been steady enough for our batch jobs, and we did not have to put a gateway in front of the store.

name: Olivia Bennett
body: RustFS gave the team an S3-compatible object store we can run ourselves. Planning capacity stayed on our hardware, and the application SDKs did not change.

name: Daniel Carter
body: The cutover plan was concrete: keep the S3 clients, change the endpoint, and validate bucket policies before traffic moved. That kept the migration review short.

name: Sophia Hayes
body: Our upload flow already used the S3 API. Switching the endpoint to RustFS was a configuration change, and object writes from the app behaved the same.

name: Michael Turner
body: Multipart upload and lifecycle rules cover the object sizes we store. I did not add a translation layer between the service and the bucket.

name: Grace Collins
body: A local RustFS container is enough for integration tests. We run the same S3 calls there that staging uses against the cluster.

name: Andrew Lawson
body: The binary and Docker installs both matched our node layout. Console health and OpenTelemetry signals are what we use for day-two checks.

name: Benjamin Reed
body: Training artifacts and table data sit in one S3-compatible store. The query tools we already had did not need a new connector.

name: Natalie Parker
body: The web console is enough to inspect buckets and objects in our review environment. We did not stand up a separate admin UI for that.

name: Lucas Mitchell
body: Erasure coding lets us set durability separately from raw capacity. The cluster model matches how we already design object storage.

name: Abigail Foster
body: We use RustFS for backups and large objects, alongside the databases, not in place of them. Versioning and lifecycle policies are the controls we rely on.

name: Chloe Simmons
body: Model checkpoints land in RustFS over the S3 API. Large-object transfers have been stable for the training jobs we run.

name: Jonathan Pierce
body: IAM, audit logging, and TLS are in the product. We can review access and destructive actions without bolting on a second control plane.

name: Ryan Gallagher
body: FTPS and S3 hit the same object store, so older transfer jobs and newer services share data. We did not add a separate protocol proxy.

name: Matthew Harper
body: Linux packages, Docker, and a single-node lab are all usable install paths. We replace the default rustfsadmin credential before a node is reachable.

name: Emily Walters
body: When a customer asks for an S3-compatible store they can run themselves, we can demo RustFS without a license server in the path.

name: Samuel Grant
body: Release artifacts go into RustFS, and the site tools already speak S3. We did not introduce a second storage API for publishing.

name: Victoria Blake
body: Apache 2.0 and self-hosting make the cost model easier to explain. We account for disks and support, not a per-request platform fee.

name: Allison Wright
body: Onboarding packets now go into a bucket with scoped access. We stopped emailing large attachments around the team.

name: Henry Dawson
body: Shared documents that used to sit on a file share now go into a versioned bucket. The console is enough for our team to retrieve them.
